rows.name: JArgs

rows.name: JArgs (option-recognition component)

Short boolean flags can be grouped, but value-taking flags have grouping restrictions.
Single-file distribution and complete platform support were not verified.

rows.name: Q2A WYSIWYG Math Editor

rows.name: Question2Answer Badges plugin

rows.name: Question2Answer

rows.reason: Question2Answer supplies a PHP/MySQL Q&A foundation with categories, tags, voting, reputation, translated interfaces and differentiated user roles, while plugins provide extension points for unmet requirements.

rows.name: Askbot

Exact multilingual workflow, report output, attachment policy and mathematical editor experience still need a version-specific check.
No quantified scalability, complete security assessment or development-time comparison was established.

rows.name: Drupal Answers
rows.application_scope: Alternative modular application composition.
rows.reason: Drupal Answers provides a modular Q&A route with accepted-answer, voting, reputation and tagging integrations when a broader CMS is also needed.

rows.name: SoapUI Open Source

rows.reason: SoapUI supplies project-based grouping, XML project portability and selective command-line test execution, making it a useful GUI candidate with an OpenAPI-version caveat.

rows.name: Portman
rows.application_scope: URL-driven collection generation and test automation.
rows.reason: Portman can fetch an OpenAPI specification URL, generate a local Postman collection and invoke Newman, covering the requested import-to-CLI path.
rows.caveat: Separate configurations and output files are a proposed grouping mechanism; GUI workspaces, licensing and historical availability were not verified.

rows.name: Milkman with HTTP and CLI plugins
rows.application_scope: Complete-client alternative for grouped REST requests, using the HTTP importer and experimental CLI. It is not presented as a proven full replacement.
rows.reason: JavaFX workbench offers workspaces, an OpenAPI importer and request CLI; exact URL import and file round trip remain unverified.
rows.caveat: OpenAPI documentation names 3.0. Direct arbitrary-URL import and workspace export/reimport are not established. CLI documents selected request execution; whole-workspace execution and Postman export are not confirmed. JavaFX addresses the Electron preference but does not prove native platform UX quality.

rows.name: OpenAPI-to-Postman with Newman
rows.application_scope: Specification conversion and file-based CLI workflow.
rows.reason: The converter creates portable request collections from OpenAPI files, while Newman supplies whole-collection and selective CLI execution.
rows.caveat: Download a URL-hosted specification before the documented converter CLI; graphical workspace editing, licensing and cutoff availability remain unverified.

rows.name: Noodle
rows.application_scope: Terminal editing and version-controlled collections.
rows.reason: Noodle combines OpenAPI import, file-based request collections, Postman export and selective CLI execution in a terminal client.
rows.caveat: Direct specification-URL input and availability at the 2020 cutoff were not established.

rows.name: SoapUI Open Source
rows.application_scope: Complete REST testing workflow using a project as a logical grouping, project XML for version control, and request-based test cases for CLI execution.
rows.reason: Best-documented grouping, file portability and selective CLI route; direct OAS URL import still needs verification.
rows.caveat: Confirm direct URL import for the exact OAS version. Open Source documentation is limited to Swagger/OAS 2.0 (older plugin text also lists 1.x); do not assume OAS 3.x. CLI operates on configured tests and project files, so arrange imported requests into test cases first. No historical feature set was verified as of 2020-01-08.

rows.name: Symfony with Symfony UX
rows.application_scope: Alternative application framework and UI integration ecosystem for rebuilding the site around retained domain behavior.
rows.reason: A PHP alternative with documented Stimulus integration and UX components offers an explicit route to charts and interactive server-rendered pages.
rows.caveat: The opened UX overview does not prove compatibility with the unseen legacy code or completion of all workflows. Custom drag/drop persistence and spreadsheet/payment integration remain necessary. Present-day notices about Symfony 6.2 maintenance must not be interpreted as its January 2023 status.

rows.name: Chart.js
rows.application_scope: Statistical chart presentation.
rows.reason: Chart.js can render graphs of backend-computed component usage counts.
rows.caveat: Does not calculate business usage metrics; inspected evidence is later than the question cutoff, and version 3.9.1 retrieval failed.

rows.name: Laravel Cashier for Stripe
rows.application_scope: Payment-provider integration.
rows.reason: Cashier's payment and subscription integration could support prepaid service purchases and account billing if Stripe matches the payment arrangement.
rows.caveat: Prepaid credits and entitlement accounting still require application logic; subscription billing is not automatically the right prepaid model.

rows.name: Vue 3 over the existing PHP/Perl backend
rows.application_scope: Frontend framework only; existing account, domain, database, export and prepaid services remain behind HTML or authenticated endpoints.
rows.reason: Incremental frontend replacement minimizes the initial backend migration surface and offers a documented path from existing server-rendered pages to richer interaction.
rows.caveat: Vue is a partial solution. Endpoint design, authorization, drag/drop synchronization, list rendering performance and the availability of reusable backend operations remain application work.

rows.name: Livewire 2
rows.application_scope: Server-driven interactive application UI.
rows.reason: Livewire's PHP-and-Blade components can implement interactive selection, forms, and group-management screens without full page reloads.
rows.caveat: Keep drag motion client-side and prototype complex editor state; versioned live documentation has no verified publication date.

rows.name: Inertia.js with Vue and Laravel
rows.application_scope: Alternative frontend architecture for a stateful drag-and-drop editor.
rows.reason: Inertia connects a Vue component-based editor to Laravel routing and controllers for richer browser-side interaction.
rows.caveat: Requires learning modern JavaScript components and a build workflow; Inertia's own opened page had no readable body, so verification relies on Laravel's primary documentation.

rows.name: Laravel 9 with Breeze
rows.application_scope: Primary PHP application framework and authentication scaffolding.
rows.reason: Laravel provides a PHP application foundation and Breeze scaffolds authentication for the site's account and database workflows.
rows.caveat: Requires modern PHP and explicit adaptation of legacy PHP/Perl logic; the starter-kit page itself is undated.

rows.name: Laravel Excel 3.1
rows.application_scope: Excel export integration.
rows.reason: Laravel Excel can turn the requesting user's selected components and groups into a downloadable Excel workbook.
rows.caveat: Export queries require user scoping, explicit columns, and memory assessment for large datasets.

rows.name: Laravel with Livewire and small JavaScript components
rows.application_scope: Primary framework stack for the rebuilt application; retain or wrap domain logic, then build account, persistence and presentation workflows around it.
rows.reason: A PHP-centered rebuild with documented reactive components is a plausible starting point for the existing PHP site, while dedicated JavaScript can handle drag-and-drop.
rows.caveat: Legacy PHP compatibility, the Perl boundary and delivery effort are unverified. Laravel 9 requires PHP 8.0 or newer; this is a documented dependency, not a contradiction because the user's runtime is unspecified. Livewire does not by itself establish the required grouping interface, thousand-item performance, prepaid flow or Excel behavior.

rows.name: Laravel with Inertia.js and Vue
rows.application_scope: Alternative full application stack to the Livewire route, using Laravel on the server and Vue for the browser interface.
rows.reason: A documented bridge combines Laravel controllers with Vue pages when the grouping workspace needs substantial client-side state.
rows.caveat: Requires learning a Vue/component workflow and asset tooling as well as handling the legacy PHP/Perl boundary. No comparative delivery-time or thousand-item interaction benchmark was obtained.

rows.name: SortableJS
rows.application_scope: Browser drag-and-drop interaction.
rows.reason: SortableJS provides cross-list dragging, grouping, and stable-ID serialization for moving components between saved groups.
rows.caveat: Persistence, account authorization, business rules, and large-list rendering remain application responsibilities.

rows.name: Django 4.1
rows.application_scope: Alternative Python application framework.
rows.reason: Django offers database models, routing, and an administrative interface as an alternative foundation for component and group management.
rows.caveat: Changing language requires translating or exposing old PHP/Perl logic, and the custom customer editor still must be built.

rows.name: Cyclos 3.6
rows.application_scope: Community payments, account management, loan and fee workflows, with third-party integration.
rows.reason: Cyclos 3.6 can provide member accounts, balances, payment authorizations, scheduled payments and loans for a community-oriented financial service.
rows.caveat: A general ledger and any required external banking connections need checking; the current official Cyclos 3 page says it is unmaintained and discourages mission-critical use, so it is a historical candidate rather than an unqualified current deployment recommendation.

rows.name: GnuCash
rows.application_scope: Accounting-only component: ledger entries, account registers and financial records.
rows.reason: GnuCash can cover the double-entry ledger and accounting portion if the credit union chooses a separate member-account and payment system.

rows.name: Mifos X
rows.application_scope: Primary core-banking shortlist: savings, loans, payment-related transfers and financial accounting.
rows.reason: Mifos X can supply the credit union's core member savings and lending operations, account transfers and integrated accounting through a configurable open-source banking platform.
rows.caveat: External payment-network connectivity and local reporting requirements still need evaluation; this research did not test a 400–1,000-member installation.

rows.name: OpenCBS Desktop
rows.application_scope: Whole candidate for client, loan, savings, payment-recording and accounting operations; evaluate Desktop/free core specifically, not the later Cloud service.
rows.reason: A plausible core-banking alternative with an open-source desktop edition, loan and savings operations, repayment recording and configurable accounting rules; the ledger boundary of the free core needs confirmation.
rows.caveat: The official repository describes Desktop development during 2013-2017. The 14.11 manual's exact date was not established. It distinguishes free-core functionality from paid modules and a configured accounting engine, so the Cloud feature matrix is not evidence for the Desktop edition. No throughput test or external clearing integration was verified.

rows.name: Cyclos 3
rows.application_scope: Whole candidate under investigation for member banking and payment operations; no claim that account histories alone satisfy the complete ledger requirement.
rows.reason: A version-specific open-source option with member accounts, payment functions and loans, but the institutional ledger requirement is unresolved and the developer now advises against mission-critical deployment.
rows.caveat: This is Cyclos 3 only. The official live page says it is no longer maintained and advises against mission-critical use. Maintenance was not an explicit user requirement, so this is a material caveat rather than an invented exclusion. Full institutional ledger coverage and exact release suitability for 400-1,000 members were not established.

rows.name: OpenCBS Desktop
rows.application_scope: Microfinance core and repayment operations, with plugin-based connections to accounting, POS and web services.
rows.reason: OpenCBS Desktop could manage clients, loans, repayments and savings while integrating a separate accounting or payment component.
rows.caveat: The opened material does not establish availability before 2014-09-15; available release files are from 2016–2017, and the live project page says Desktop is unsupported after replacement by Cloud in 2019.

rows.name: S.A.F.E. Open Source Microfinance Suite
rows.application_scope: Integrated microfinance suite; present-day project listing includes loan, cashier, accounting, savings and bank modules.
rows.reason: SAFE offers a microfinance-oriented starting point for combining lending, cash handling, savings and accounting in a small financial institution.
rows.caveat: The June 2014 release notes warn of difficult configuration and partial English translation; the live module list is later evidence and does not establish that every named module existed in the 2014 release.

rows.name: Mifos X
rows.application_scope: Whole candidate for the credit union's operational core, using Mifos X's own open-source platform and interface; no proprietary mLite front end is assumed.
rows.reason: The strongest starting point for an open-source core: dated project material documents lending, integrated accounting and savings, with the exact payment workflow and 2014 configuration still to verify.
rows.caveat: The 2013 initial release was individual-lending oriented. A July 2013 article documents savings and MPL 2.0 but has a December 2014 modification timestamp. Payment integrations cannot be inferred from a proprietary M-Pesa application. The 1.25 repayment/accrual announcement is after the question. Exact 400-1,000-member deployment sizing and institution-specific workflows were not tested.

rows.name: yt-dlp
rows.application_scope: URL acquisition component; combine with a local editor.
rows.reason: yt-dlp supplies the free YouTube-URL download step for a desktop workflow, after which the saved video can be trimmed and joined in LosslessCut.
rows.caveat: It is a command-line downloader rather than a visual editor; section downloading needs FFmpeg, and concatenating selected sections still requires an editing/joining step.

rows.name: Flixier
rows.application_scope: Integrated browser workflow for a study gist within the free export allowance.
rows.reason: The best-documented browser fit: YouTube-link import, trimming and joining, and a downloadable result are available on a capped free plan.
rows.caveat: Free tier is 720p, watermarked, and limited to 10 exported minutes per month. URL ingestion is documented but was not tested. One YouTube-specific page now redirects to a generic page; another live official page still explicitly documents YouTube URLs.

rows.name: LosslessCut
rows.application_scope: Desktop trimming and joining component paired with yt-dlp for YouTube input.
rows.reason: LosslessCut lets the user keep selected portions of a downloaded video and merge those cut segments into a shorter local file without re-encoding.
rows.caveat: A separate downloader supplies the YouTube input; the tool emphasizes rough cuts, and lossless merging requires compatible codecs; use the free manual downloads rather than assuming every store listing is free.

rows.name: Cut/Storm
rows.application_scope: Potential whole workflow, not yet confirmed; locally hosted browser app requiring Docker.
rows.reason: A free self-hosted URL-import and trimming option remains provisional because joining arbitrary separated sections is not established.
rows.caveat: The README documents one-video editing, in/out trimming and MP4 output, but not arbitrary multi-section joining. Default URL duration limit is 900 seconds. Docker setup would be additional work.

rows.name: Flixier
rows.application_scope: Complete browser workflow for occasional shorter study summaries.
rows.reason: Flixier documents importing a YouTube link directly into its browser editor, cutting and combining useful clips, and exporting the assembled video to a computer.
rows.caveat: The current free tier allows ten export minutes per month at 720p with a watermark and 2 GB storage; cutoff-date availability of these exact features and limits remains unverified.

rows.name: Kapwing
rows.application_scope: Complete browser workflow for a short study digest.
rows.reason: Kapwing offers a browser timeline for importing a YouTube URL, trimming and rearranging selected portions, then downloading the resulting short video.
rows.caveat: The current free plan exports at 720p with a watermark and a four-minute limit; exact plan terms as of 2023-07-19 were not established, and no live edit/export was tested.

rows.name: WonderFox Free HD Video Converter Factory
rows.application_scope: Desktop fallback using the app's Downloader and Converter modules to acquire a source, retain clips, merge and save.
rows.reason: A Windows fallback combines a YouTube-URL downloader with free trim, merge, and local output features in one application.
rows.caveat: Windows-specific. Use the Free edition. Documentation is from after the question date, and the workflow has not been executed.

rows.name: Cutlab
rows.application_scope: Integrated browser workflow for publicly accessible, non-age-restricted YouTube videos of at most 30 minutes.
rows.reason: A free browser alternative documents direct YouTube imports and a timeline for trimming, arranging clips, and exporting a local video.
rows.caveat: URL fetching can fail; private, age-restricted, and over-30-minute sources are unsupported. Export is real-time and the tab must stay open; output is MP4 where supported, otherwise WebM. No practical run was performed.

rows.name: OGDF (Open Graph Drawing Framework)
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; graph/data-structure layer can be used without making visualization the task
rows.reason: A documented C++ graph library with broad structural mutation and associated attributes; its adjacency-list representation and GPL terms introduce concrete tradeoffs to evaluate.
rows.caveat: The opened API is 2023.09, after the question date. Full Boost dependency closure and requested performance are unverified. Edge lookup is degree-dependent. GPL v2/v3 with exceptions may fit the license preference less well.

rows.name: SNAP (Stanford Network Analysis Platform)
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; choose directed/undirected graph and richer network containers according to semantics
rows.reason: Best documented broad fit found: self-contained C++ graph/network containers with dynamic structure, rich node/edge data, and explicit large-network design.
rows.caveat: Uses its own GLib-style types. Modern C++11 idioms, filtered-query performance, exact move semantics and strongly skewed-degree performance were not established. Benchmark the concrete workload.

rows.name: LEMON
rows.application_scope: whole C++ graph-library alternative; investigate mutable ListGraph/ListDigraph rather than assuming every representation supports all edits
rows.reason: A promising C++ graph-library alternative with permissive source licensing and indexed evidence of mutable ListGraph/ListDigraph APIs, but several required properties could not be fully verified.
rows.caveat: Official tutorial and graph documentation opens were blocked; attempted source-file opens also failed. Significant-Boost-dependency absence, degree behavior, performance, and exact semantics remain unverified. Boost Software License is a license name, not evidence of Boost code use.

rows.name: NetworKit C++ core
rows.application_scope: Sparse-network analysis, graph iteration, directed/undirected conversion, and parallel algorithms.
rows.reason: NetworKit provides a native C++ graph-analysis core with historical support for directed graphs and indexed edge attributes, making it a useful candidate when scalable traversal and analytics dominate.
rows.caveat: The project emphasizes analytics and Python integration; exact historical mutation costs, high-degree deletion behavior, arbitrary payload ergonomics, and absence of significant Boost dependencies were not fully verified. Present-day storage/API additions must not be assumed available in 2016.

rows.name: LLAMA — mutable multiversioned CSR graph storage
rows.application_scope: Storage-mechanism alternative for large graphs, consistent analytical snapshots, and optional out-of-memory operation.
rows.reason: LLAMA is a C++11 storage alternative that combines updates with compact CSR snapshots and node/edge properties for workloads that alternate incoming changes with whole-graph analysis.
rows.caveat: This is a research-oriented storage engine rather than a simple drop-in graph container; the README flags unfinished streaming integration and a broken persistent deletion configuration. A complete directed/undirected convenience API and arbitrary mutation behavior were not verified.

rows.name: SNAP — Stanford Network Analysis Platform
rows.application_scope: Large in-memory networks with traversal, filtering/subgraph extraction, and custom semantics on nodes or edges.
rows.reason: SNAP supplies directed and undirected graphs, mutable network operations, and templated vertex/edge data types for large sparse-network analysis.
rows.caveat: Its custom GLib containers, pointers, and iterator conventions are an integration commitment rather than a modern standard-library-style API; historical releases include breaking changes and deletion fixes. No workload-specific performance or full dependency/license audit was performed.

rows.name: OGDF — Open Graph Drawing Framework
rows.application_scope: General graph algorithms and representation, with particular strength in planarity, decomposition, graph drawing, and associated metadata.
rows.reason: OGDF offers a self-contained C++ graph representation, node/edge associative arrays, and reusable graph algorithms for applications that also benefit from topology manipulation or drawing.
rows.caveat: GPL licensing conflicts with the preference for a permissive license, and a drawing-oriented library may add unnecessary scope. The opened material does not establish favorable allocation behavior or performance for this particular mutation-heavy workload.

rows.name: LEMON — ListDigraph/ListGraph with selectable graph representations
rows.application_scope: General-purpose in-process graph storage and algorithms; List types for mutation, Smart types for append-oriented use, StaticDigraph for fixed directed graphs.
rows.reason: LEMON offers mutable directed and undirected graph types, maps for associated data, and alternative representations that directly address the tradeoff between flexible updates and compact traversal.
rows.caveat: Smart types do not support arbitrary deletion and StaticDigraph is immutable; mutations can invalidate affected iterators and removed IDs may be reused. C++11 style, complete dependency/license verification, and the exact version publication date remain unverified in the opened evidence.

rows.name: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct
rows.application_scope: Local model component for coding chat and agentic editing.
rows.reason: This open-weight coding model offers documented local serving, long context and Cline-oriented tool support as a backend candidate for repository-level coding tasks.
rows.caveat: Its 30.5B total parameters and context cache require substantial memory despite only 3.3B active parameters; parity with GPT-5 or Claude was not established.

rows.name: Kilo Code with its local Ollama provider
rows.application_scope: Overall agent alternative being evaluated; local agent requests are documented, while complete local feature parity remains unresolved.
rows.reason: A second open-source VS Code agent with explicit local configuration, but the all-local autocomplete story is not established for the current version.
caveat: Set the main and small models locally and prevent Gateway fallback.

Current configuration instructions tell users to use Mistral BYOK or disable autocomplete; a separate feature-page search result claims local autocomplete, so version/configuration alignment is unresolved.
The project source distinguishes main and v2 development; do not mix settings across versions.
Local inference speed and tool behavior still require a project trial.

rows.name: Cline with Ollama or LM Studio
rows.application_scope: Multi-file generation, debugging and refactoring with reviewable changes.
rows.reason: Cline supplies a VS Code agent that can coordinate file changes, run commands and inspect errors while using a locally served model.
rows.caveat: Local-model capability and memory requirements remain decisive; an open-source extension does not make hosted inference unlimited.

rows.name: Cline with Ollama and a local Qwen3-Coder model
rows.application_scope: Overall VS Code agent alternative for repository tasks; configure a local Ollama backend. Inline completion is not established by the inspected Cline sources.
rows.reason: The clearest documented VS Code route for coordinated file edits and local model inference; benchmark quality and speed on the client's project before relying on it.
caveat: No firsthand project run was performed.
Hardware, acceptable response time and model-specific tool-call reliability are unknown.
The document-supported route does not prove GPT-5/Claude-equivalent results or reliable large-codebase work.

rows.name: Continue with a local Ollama backend
rows.application_scope: VS Code completion, chat and edits using models served locally.
rows.reason: Continue can connect VS Code to local models with separate completion, chat and editing roles, providing a configurable starting point for the requested editor workflow.
rows.caveat: Hardware and model quality set practical limits; reliable agent mode also requires working tool support.

rows.name: Tabby self-hosted server and VS Code extension
rows.application_scope: Self-hosted completion and codebase assistance, including shared-server deployments.
rows.reason: Tabby supplies a self-hosted VS Code completion, code-question and inline-editing service that can centralize inference on hardware controlled by the developer or team.
rows.caveat: Requires operating a server and choosing its models; the opened client documentation did not establish a full autonomous multi-file agent workflow.

rows.name: Continue with local Ollama models
rows.application_scope: Overall VS Code assistant candidate; separate local models can fill chat/edit/apply, autocomplete and embedding roles.
rows.reason: A documented local chat/edit/completion route, with a significant current maintenance caveat and unverified end-to-end multi-file agent suitability.
caveat: Current official repository states that it is no longer actively maintained and describes a final 2.0.0 release.
Active maintenance was not an explicit user must, so this is a caveat rather than a mandatory exclusion.
Compatibility of the final extension, the chosen runtime/model and full agent workflow is untested.
The Ollama guide's relevant text was seen in search excerpts; its initial opened excerpt did not expose the body.

rows.name: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct
rows.application_scope: Model/backend component for a VS Code extension, not an editor assistant by itself.
rows.reason: A concrete first local-model trial because its official card names Cline/tool support and Kilo's local guide recommends its 30B variant.
caveat: 30.5B total weights, despite 3.3B active per token; actual memory depends on precision, runtime and context.
Native 262144-token support is a model specification, not a guarantee that the user's hardware can serve that context.
No measured equivalence to GPT-5/Claude or success rate on this client repository is established.

rows.name: Aider with a local Ollama model
rows.application_scope: Terminal-based coding on a project with a configurable local model.
rows.reason: Aider provides a documented local-model project-editing workflow that can be used from VS Code's integrated terminal when a terminal-first assistant is acceptable.
rows.caveat: This is an alternative interaction style; native inline completion was not verified, and model editing reliability and context sizing need evaluation.

rows.name: jQuery formBuilder with formRender
rows.application_scope: Form-authoring and form-rendering components; author supplies PHP definition storage and answer-processing endpoints, PDF creation and email.
rows.reason: An MIT-licensed visual designer and renderer can be embedded in the existing application, with documented definition and response APIs that map to the author's PHP backend.
rows.caveat: Entirely client-side components. The onSave example uses session storage and must be changed to a server request; server validation, permissions and durable storage are application work.

rows.name: jQuery formBuilder with formRender
rows.application_scope: Lightweight frontend form editor and renderer embedded in the existing application.
rows.reason: This MIT-licensed JavaScript component can give the client a drag-and-drop editor and render saved JSON/XML form definitions while a custom PHP endpoint handles submissions.
rows.caveat: Not a complete hosted form service; the application must store definitions, handle submissions, validate server-side, and provide email/PDF delivery; depends on jQuery; direct implementation-source open failed, but source-tree documentation was opened.

rows.name: SurveyJS Survey Creator with Form Library
rows.application_scope: JavaScript designer and renderer inside the management application; PHP backend uses the documented JSON definition and submission workflow.
rows.reason: A documented visual-authoring-to-PHP workflow covers saved form definitions and submitted answers, but the designer is paid and the user's acceptable one-off budget is unspecified.
rows.caveat: Do not confuse the free renderer with the paid Creator. Current Basic price observed at US$559 once per developer; 2025 price and user's affordability threshold are unknown. Backend endpoints remain developer work.

rows.name: Reef Form Generator
rows.application_scope: Embedded authoring, rendering, and local storage.
rows.reason: Reef supplies an embeddable PHP/JavaScript drag-and-drop form editor plus validation and PDO storage, so the client can edit forms while the existing management application receives submissions.
rows.caveat: LGPL 3.0; application supplies access control and email/PDF integration; runtime compatibility unverified; complex custom forms are outside its intended emphasis.

rows.name: OpnForm
rows.application_scope: Separate Laravel/Nuxt form application.
rows.reason: OpnForm's self-hostable visual builder, email notifications, and webhooks could collect client-edited forms and forward answers to the management application.
rows.caveat: Verify self-hosted licensing and respondent access; operating a full application adds deployment work.

rows.name: SurveyJS Survey Creator with Form Library
rows.application_scope: Custom integrated form-authoring experience with saved schemas, dynamic forms, and application-controlled submission storage.
rows.reason: SurveyJS provides an embeddable visual editor that saves JSON form definitions and a renderer that can submit responses to the existing PHP backend under the application's own access rules.
rows.caveat: The renderer is free, but embedded Survey Creator requires a paid license; current Basic pricing is $559 per developer, with optional update/support renewal, and the PDF generator belongs to a higher tier; backend/email integration is still required.

rows.name: MachForm Self-Hosted
rows.application_scope: Separate self-hosted form-building application; booking forms, data collection, email/PDF delivery, and HTTP integration.
rows.reason: MachForm provides a ready-made PHP/MySQL visual form builder with email notifications, PDF attachments, and HTTP webhooks, covering client editing and reception delivery with limited custom plumbing.
rows.caveat: Commercial software; live homepage advertises a $99 one-time self-hosted license, which is not a verified February 2025 price; confirm license tier and test public respondent access and integration before purchase.

rows.name: OpnForm

rows.name: WebAuthn Level 2 public-key authentication

rows.name: RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
